title: Bernanke sets different tests for slowing purchases and raising rates
summary: A payroll gain could bring the Federal Reserve closer to buying fewer bonds while leaving the case for a rate increase little changed. That distinction runs through Ben Bernanke’s written testimony to Congress on 22 May. The Federal Open Market Committee was buying $45 billion of longer-term Treasuries and $40 billion of agency mortgage-backed securities each month. The Chair described how incoming news could change the purchase pace in either direction. The separate guidance on the federal funds rate allowed accommodation to persist well after purchases ended. A portfolio exposed to the ten-year Treasury and one exposed to the next overnight rate decision therefore faced different policy questions on the same morning. (Monetary Policy.)

The Chair gave Congress enough labour-market evidence to understand why a change in one instrument could precede a change in the other. Monthly payroll growth had accelerated to more than 200,000 on average over six months. Yet a fall in measured unemployment could reflect people leaving the labour force as well as people finding work. Almost eight million people wanted full-time hours and worked part-time. A business that lengthens shifts before hiring can improve household income even while headcount growth slows. Conversely, a falling unemployment rate alongside declining participation can overstate the improvement. A researcher assessing the purchase programme would have to decide whether the better news made continued gains more likely, as the programme’s test concerned the labour-market outlook. (Current Economic Conditions; Monetary Policy.)

The rate guidance imposed a different discipline. Unemployment of 6.5% was one condition in a description of how long the Committee expected the near-zero target to remain appropriate. It sat alongside a conditional inflation projection and a requirement that longer-run inflation expectations remain anchored. Even a faster approach to the unemployment threshold left considerable discretion. The prior twelve months’ PCE inflation was just 1%, and Bernanke saw a risk that inflation could have been lower without monetary support. A researcher who codes a faster pace of hiring as an unqualified signal of higher near-term short rates discards the price-stability side of the decision. (Current Economic Conditions; Monetary Policy.)

Fiscal policy was another reason to be careful about extrapolating the payroll numbers. The testimony cited a Congressional Budget Office estimate that the deficit-reduction measures then in law would lower 2013 GDP growth by about 1½ percentage points relative to the counterfactual. That estimate describes the difference between two paths for output growth. Subtracting it from an already published growth forecast that includes the measures would count the restraint twice. Bernanke thought monetary policy had limited capacity to offset it with short rates already close to zero. Housing was a particularly important counterweight. Lower mortgage rates could support home purchases, construction jobs and household wealth, giving the composition of bond purchases economic significance beyond the programme’s total dollar amount. (Fiscal Policy, including footnote 1; Monetary Policy.)

Bernanke also put a time horizon on the costs of accommodation. Investors seeking income could take on duration, leverage or credit risk; savers depending on interest income were already bearing a cost. Raising rates early could improve the nominal return available for a short period while weakening the activity and inflation that would support higher rates over several years. That argument points to two distinct empirical questions: whether investors were taking more risk at prevailing yields, and whether the private recovery could withstand less support. High asset prices alone settle neither question. Finally, this source is prepared congressional testimony. Its scope ends before the exchange with legislators. A study of the hearing’s price impact needs a separate record of that exchange and its timestamps before assigning a market move to a particular remark. (Monetary Policy.)

questions.question: Which labour indicators would have justified a slower purchase pace at the time?
questions.detail: Reconstruct the vintages of payrolls, the participation rate, involuntary part-time employment and inflation available on the testimony date. Compare their signals with the subsequent revisions. A slowdown in purchases was conditional on a sustained improvement in the outlook. Using the final revised series can make that improvement appear visible several months before a policymaker could have observed it.

questions.question: Did investors revise their expectations of purchases or of the first rate increase?
questions.detail: Separate the prepared release from the start of questioning, then compare short-dated interest-rate futures with longer Treasuries and agency mortgage spreads in each verified window. A large move at the long end alongside little change in the next meetings would motivate a duration or later-policy-path explanation. Distinguishing those two channels would require more evidence, including expectations of future short rates.

questions.question: How much of the housing recovery depended on the transmission from mortgages to household cash flow?
questions.detail: Compare refinancing volumes and the rates actually paid by borrowers across groups with different eligibility and existing mortgage coupons. Then look for changes in spending or construction as financing costs shift. A fall in a quoted mortgage rate measures the price on a new contract; the effect on household cash flow also depends on who can take it up and when.
